title: TCP Congestion Control
summary: Specifies the four congestion control algorithms TCP uses to avoid overwhelming the network: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery. It also covers how to resume sending after an idle period and some guidance on generating acknowledgments. It is a Draft Standard on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5681 explains how TCP adjusts its sending rate to share network capacity and respond to packet loss. It defines rules for starting transmission, increasing the amount of data in flight, and reducing it when congestion appears.

subtitle: The rules TCP uses to limit sending, respond to loss and avoid overwhelming a shared network.

tldr.problem: A TCP sender cannot know the network's available capacity in advance. Sending too much can add congestion, so the sender needs rules for controlling data in flight and reacting to loss.
tldr.mechanism: TCP limits outstanding data with a congestion window, grows that window with slow start and congestion avoidance, and reduces sending after loss. Three duplicate acknowledgments can trigger fast retransmit without waiting for a timeout.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5681 obsoletes RFC 2581 and has Internet Standard status in the unit metadata. It has been updated by RFC 9438.

sections.title: Four TCP Congestion Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 5681 specifies four related TCP congestion-control algorithms: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery. Together, they control how much data a sender puts into the network and how it responds when data appears to be lost.

The RFC also covers restarting after a long idle period and how a receiver generates acknowledgments. Its algorithms use packet loss as a signal of congestion; Explicit Congestion Notification is discussed as another possible signal in RFC 3168.

The document says a sender may be more cautious than these rules, but it MUST NOT send more aggressively than they allow.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP uses four rules to manage sending: start carefully, increase the sending limit, resend data when loss is likely, and manage sending during recovery. These rules help TCP react when the network is congested.

sections.title: The Sender and Receiver Windows
sections.content:
The congestion window (cwnd) limits how much data the sender may have sent without receiving acknowledgments. The receiver window (rwnd) is the receiver's advertised limit. A sender must obey whichever of these two limits is smaller.

The sender maximum segment size (SMSS) is the largest segment it can send, excluding TCP/IP headers and options. Flight size is the amount of sent data that has not yet been cumulatively acknowledged. The slow start threshold (ssthresh) selects whether slow start or congestion avoidance controls window growth.

A duplicate acknowledgment meets specific conditions, including that it acknowledges no new data and repeats the greatest acknowledgment number already received. A TCP using Selective Acknowledgment can also use new SACK information to identify a duplicate acknowledgment.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender has one limit based on network congestion and another based on what the receiver can accept. It must stay within the smaller limit.

sections.title: Slow Start and Congestion Avoidance
sections.content:
Slow start and congestion avoidance are required for TCP senders. TCP uses slow start while cwnd is below ssthresh, congestion avoidance while it is above the threshold, and may use either when they are equal.

At the beginning of a transfer, slow start probes available capacity. For each acknowledgment of new data, it increases cwnd by no more than SMSS bytes. The recommended byte-counting rule increases it by the smaller of the newly acknowledged byte count and SMSS, which reduces the effect of a receiver splitting acknowledgments.

During congestion avoidance, the window grows by about one full-sized segment per round-trip time and MUST NOT grow by more than SMSS bytes per round-trip time. After a retransmission timeout signals loss, ssthresh is reduced based on FlightSize and cwnd is set to no more than one full-sized segment.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP begins with a small sending limit and increases it as acknowledgments arrive. It increases more carefully after the slow-start threshold, and cuts back when a timeout signals loss.

sections.title: Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery
sections.content:
A receiver SHOULD send an immediate duplicate acknowledgment when it gets an out-of-order segment. Three duplicate acknowledgments without an intervening acknowledgment of new data indicate a likely loss, so the sender retransmits the missing segment without waiting for its retransmission timer.

Fast recovery controls sending until an acknowledgment covers new data. The sender reduces its threshold, retransmits the missing segment and temporarily adjusts its congestion window to account for segments that have left the network. It can send new data only when the congestion and receiver windows allow it.

When an acknowledgment for new data arrives, the sender sets cwnd to ssthresh. The RFC notes that this method does not recover efficiently when multiple segments are lost in one flight, and recommends implementing an advanced loss-recovery algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Three repeated acknowledgments for the same data suggest that a segment is missing. TCP resends it immediately, then controls sending until new data is acknowledged.

sections.title: Idle Connections and Acknowledgments
sections.content:
After a connection has been idle longer than the retransmission timeout, a sender SHOULD reduce cwnd to no more than the restart window before sending again. The restart window is the smaller of the initial window and the current congestion window.

A receiver SHOULD use delayed acknowledgments without delaying them excessively. It SHOULD acknowledge at least every second full-sized segment and MUST acknowledge within 500 milliseconds of the first unacknowledged packet arriving. It SHOULD acknowledge out-of-order data and data that fills a gap immediately.

A receiver MUST NOT send more than one acknowledgment per incoming segment, except to update the advertised window as the application consumes data.
sections.plainLanguage: After a long pause, TCP reduces its sending limit before starting again. A receiver also needs to send acknowledgments often enough to keep the sender informed.

sections.title: Security and Network Stability
sections.content:
An attacker who causes data or acknowledgments to be lost can make a TCP connection slow down. Forged duplicate acknowledgments can also affect the sender's rate.

The opposite behavior can be more damaging: forged acknowledgments for new data or excessive duplicate acknowledgments can make endpoints send too aggressively. The RFC warns that this could drive part of the network into congestion collapse.

Byte counting, which bases window growth on the amount of newly acknowledged data rather than a fixed increase per acknowledgment, helps resist acknowledgment-division attacks. The RFC says Internet stability depends considerably on correct implementation of these algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: False acknowledgments can make a sender slow down or send too much. Correct window updates help prevent one connection from pushing its share of traffic too high.
